section.title: Encouragement to Faithfulness
section.sectionRationale: The letter opens with Paul, an aging apostle in a Roman prison facing death, writing to his beloved son in the faith. Before any hard charge, he grounds Timothy in grace: a heritage of sincere faith, a gift of God to be stirred up, a gospel worth suffering for, and a good deposit worth guarding. The chapter moves from tender thanksgiving to a ringing call not to be ashamed, and it ends with living examples of both desertion and loyalty.
section.thesis: Because God has saved and called us by His own grace and has given us a Spirit of power, love, and self-control, we need not be ashamed of the gospel or its prisoners; instead we fan the gift into flame and guard the good deposit, trusting the One who keeps what we entrust to Him.
section.frameNote: Four movements within the chapter: the greeting and thanksgiving for Timothy's sincere faith; the call to fan the gift into flame and not shrink back in fear; the summons to share in suffering for a gospel of grace and to guard the deposit; and the contrast between those who deserted Paul and faithful Onesiphorus.

verses.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus,
To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
I thank God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as did my forefathers, as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers.
Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy.
I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well.
For this reason I remind you to {{anazopyreo|fan into flame}} the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands.
For God has not given us a spirit of {{deilia|fear}}, but of power, love, and self-control.

units.label: Do not be ashamed of the gospel

verses.text: So do not be {{epaischynomai|ashamed}} of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God.
He has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began.
And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel,
to which I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher.
For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.
Hold on to the {{hypotyposis|pattern}} of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
Guard the {{paratheke|treasure entrusted}} to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.
You know that everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes.
May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains.
Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me.
May the Lord grant Onesiphorus His mercy on that day. You know very well how much he ministered to me in Ephesus.

anazopyreo.gloss: To rekindle, to fan a fire back into full flame. The picture is of embers that are still alive but need stirring so they blaze again. Paul is not saying Timothy has lost his gift, but that grace-given gifts must be actively stoked, not left to smolder. Faithfulness is not passive; it keeps the coals bright.

deilia.gloss: Timidity, cowardice, a shrinking fearfulness. It is the only place this word appears in the New Testament, and it names the very thing that would keep Timothy quiet and ashamed. Against it Paul sets a threefold gift of the Spirit: power, love, and self-control. The footnote to the verse offers timidity or cowardice as the sense.

epaischynomai.gloss: To be ashamed of, to feel disgrace over. It runs like a thread through the chapter: do not be ashamed of the testimony, I am not ashamed, and Onesiphorus was not ashamed of my chains. In a culture where a chained prisoner was a public embarrassment, Paul calls loyalty to Christ and His servants a matter of holy courage.

hypotyposis.gloss: A pattern, outline, or model to be copied. Timothy is to hold the sound words he heard from Paul as a fixed standard, a form of teaching that shapes everything else. The apostolic gospel is not raw material to be reinvented but a trustworthy template to be preserved and passed on.

paratheke.gloss: A deposit, something valuable placed in another's trust for safekeeping. The same word stands behind what I have entrusted to Him in verse 12 and the treasure entrusted to you in verse 14. God guards what we entrust to Him, and we guard the gospel He entrusts to us; the good deposit is kept safe only with the help of the indwelling Spirit.

basic.context: Paul is in prison in Rome, near the end of his life, writing to Timothy, his younger co-worker whom he loves like a son. Before he gives any hard instructions, he encourages Timothy: he thanks God for the genuine faith Timothy learned from his grandmother and mother, reminds him to stir up God's gift in him, and urges him not to be ashamed of Jesus or of Paul the prisoner, but to be ready to suffer for the good news.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a personal letter, but its call is for every believer: do not be ashamed of Christ, and guard the gospel you have received. Paul intends Timothy to act, to fan the gift into flame and hold the pattern of sound teaching, which shows that faithfulness is something we pursue, leaning on the Holy Spirit rather than on our own nerve.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul tells Timothy to anazopyreo, to fan into flame, the gift of God. He says God did not give a spirit of deilia, timidity or cowardice, but of power, love, and self-control. He is to hold the hypotyposis, the pattern, of sound teaching, and to guard the paratheke, the good deposit, the same word for what Paul has entrusted to God for safekeeping.
basic.typology: Timothy's faith handed down through Lois and Eunice pictures how God preserves His truth across generations. The good deposit guarded by the Spirit looks forward to the whole church keeping the gospel until Christ returns.
basic.christ: Christ Jesus is our Savior who has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. This grace was given us in Him before time began and revealed in His appearing. He is the One Paul trusts to guard the deposit safely until that day.
basic.god: God saves and calls us not because of our works but by His own purpose and grace, planned before the ages. He gives His Spirit of power, love, and self-control, and He is able to keep safe everything we entrust to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 1 shows Paul unashamed of the gospel because it is God's power for salvation. Ephesians 2 echoes salvation by grace, not works. First Timothy 6 also charges Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him.
basic.oneStory: God's plan of grace in Christ was set before time began, revealed when Christ appeared, and is now entrusted to His servants to pass on. Timothy stands in a line of faithful people, from Lois and Eunice to Paul, carrying the deposit forward until the day Christ returns.

context.literary:
Second Timothy 1 is built as a letter opening that keeps widening. Verses 1 and 2 give the standard Pauline address, with 'mercy' added between grace and peace, as in 1 Timothy 1:2. Verses 3 to 5 are a thanksgiving that turns on memory: Paul remembers Timothy in prayer, remembers his tears, and is reminded of his faith. The verbs of remembering then become commands. 'For this reason' opens verse 6, and the same phrase opens verse 12, so the chapter has two hinges, each of which turns a fact about God or Paul into an instruction for Timothy.

Three phrases about shame mark the chapter's spine. Timothy is told not to be ashamed in verse 8. Paul declares he is not ashamed in verse 12. Onesiphorus is praised in verse 16 as one who was not ashamed of Paul's chains. A command, a testimony and an example are placed in that order, so that Timothy meets the instruction, then the apostle who obeys it, then an ordinary believer who does the same.

Verses 9 and 10 are a compact statement of the gospel, with its balanced clauses about what God did before time and what He has now revealed. Many scholars hear in it a fragment of early Christian tradition, though that cannot be proved; what is clear is that Paul drops it into the middle of an exhortation as the ground on which the exhortation stands. The verb 'guard' appears twice, in verse 12 of what Paul has handed to God and in verse 14 of what has been handed to Timothy, so the two guardianships are deliberately set side by side. The chapter closes with a contrast of two groups, those in Asia who left and one household that stayed.
context.historical:
Paul writes from Rome, as verse 17 says, and he is in chains, verses 8 and 16, facing the end of his life. Most readers place this second Roman imprisonment in the mid sixties, after Nero's persecution had made a Christian prisoner a dangerous person to be seen with. In that setting 'ashamed' is not about embarrassment alone. A prisoner of the empire carried public disgrace, and to visit him, write to him or own his message could cost a person reputation, freedom or life.

Timothy came from Lystra, in Asia Minor, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, Acts 16:1-3. Luke records that Paul met him there and took him along, and the household of Lois and Eunice is the first picture we have of a family where Scripture was taught. Later in this same letter Paul says Timothy had known the Holy Scriptures 'from infancy,' 2 Timothy 3:15. For most of his service Timothy has been Paul's delegate, and at the time of this letter he appears to be in Ephesus, the city where Onesiphorus once served Paul, verse 18.

The Roman province of Asia, whose capital was Ephesus, was the heartland of Paul's earlier ministry. His statement that 'everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me,' verse 15, should be read as a painful summary of the believers who had been in a position to stand with him in Rome, not as a claim that every Christian there had apostatised. Phygelus and Hermogenes are named only here in the New Testament; we know nothing more of them. The laying on of hands, verse 6, was the practice by which a gift and a task were recognised and blessed, and 1 Timothy 4:14 shows the elders sharing in it.
context.canonical:
The chapter's central refusal of shame draws on a thread that runs through the whole canon. Psalm after psalm prays not to be put to shame while trusting in the Lord, and Isaiah 28:16 promises that 'the one who believes will never be shaken.' Paul's own earlier boast, 'I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation,' Romans 1:16, is the same confession from a freer season. Behind both stands Jesus' warning that he who is ashamed of Him and His words will find the Son of Man ashamed of him, Mark 8:38, and the writer to the Hebrews looks to the One who endured the cross, 'scorning its shame,' Hebrews 12:2.

Verses 9 and 10 gather themes that are told elsewhere in fuller form. Election 'before time began' appears in Titus 1:2, Ephesians 1:4 and 1 Peter 1:20. Salvation 'not because of our works' echoes Ephesians 2:8-9 and Titus 3:5. The victory over death belongs to the story told in 1 Corinthians 15, where death is 'the last enemy to be destroyed,' verse 26, and 'swallowed up in victory,' verse 54.

The idea of a deposit is taken up in 1 Timothy 6:20 and in the final charge of this very letter, 2 Timothy 4:1-8, where Paul looks back and says he has kept the faith. The Spirit who gives power rather than fear stands opposite the 'spirit of slavery that returns you to fear' in Romans 8:15, and answers the promise of Acts 1:8 that the disciples would receive power when the Spirit came. Paul's trusting entrusting of himself to God echoes 1 Peter 4:19, where those who suffer are told to entrust their souls to their faithful Creator.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes as a dying man to a younger leader who is tempted to retreat. He does not scold; he builds a case. He reminds Timothy of his family, his calling and the hands laid on him, so that Timothy will remember that his ministry was given to him by God and affirmed by the church, and was never his own invention. He then removes the excuse that suffering means failure by pointing at Paul himself, who is chained and yet unashamed.

The two verbs that carry the practical weight are 'fan' and 'guard.' Timothy is not to invent a new message or a new gift, nor to drift in neutral. He is to keep a fire burning and keep a treasure safe. Paul also wants Timothy to see that this is not grim self reliance. The Spirit who dwells in them is named as the one who helps Timothy guard, verse 14, and the power for suffering is 'the power of God,' verse 8.

Finally, Paul wants Timothy to notice people. The chapter ends with those who walked away and the one man who walked toward Paul. A leader's courage is formed partly by the friends he chooses to be seen with, and Paul asks Timothy to be a man like Onesiphorus.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter mixes description and instruction, and it helps to keep them apart. The story of Lois and Eunice, the abandonment in Asia, and the visit of Onesiphorus are descriptions of what happened to real people. They are not commands that every grandmother must produce a pastor, or that every believer will be deserted. What they offer is a pattern, a household that handed on faith and a friend who risked association with a prisoner.

The commands are plain and still apply: do not be ashamed of Christ or of His suffering people, share in suffering for the gospel, hold the pattern of sound teaching, and guard the entrusted treasure with the help of the Spirit. The laying on of hands in verse 6 is a particular act that happened to Timothy through Paul. It should not be turned into a rule that a gift is only real when a certain person's hands have been laid on someone. What carries over is the principle that gifts are received, recognised by the church and kept alive by use, and that fear is not a fitting response to the gift of a God who gives power, love and self-control.

debates.question: What is the 'gift of God' that Timothy is to fan into flame?

views.label: A particular ministry gift or office
views.case: Paul says the gift came through the laying on of his hands, verse 6, and 1 Timothy 4:14 speaks of a gift given with a prophecy and the laying on of hands by the elders. On this view the gift is Timothy's equipping for pastoral teaching and leadership, which he must now exercise rather than let fall idle.

views.label: The Holy Spirit Himself
views.case: The next verse speaks of the spirit God gave 'us,' and verse 14 mentions the Spirit who dwells in us. Some readers hold that the gift is the Spirit's presence and power, and that fanning it means yielding to Him. The shift from 'the gift' to 'a spirit of fear' versus power, love and self-control supports a link between gift and Spirit.

views.label: Both together
views.case: A third reading refuses the choice. Whatever the specific ministry equipment was, it came by the Spirit, so the gift is a Spirit given capacity for service. This is the most common middle position, and it fits both verses.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the command is the same: the gift is received, not earned, and yet it needs tending. Paul grounds courage in what God has already given and not in Timothy's temperament.

debates.question: What is the 'deposit' that Paul says God is able to guard?

views.label: What Paul has entrusted to God, his own life and soul
views.case: Verse 12 reads 'what I have entrusted to Him for that day,' and the context is Paul's suffering. This reading takes the phrase as Paul's trust that God will keep him safe through trial and judgment, and finds support in 1 Peter 4:19 and in Paul's own confidence in 2 Timothy 4:18.

views.label: What God has entrusted to Paul, the gospel
views.case: The same Greek word is used in verse 14 and in 1 Timothy 6:20 of the gospel committed to Timothy. If the word means the same thing in verse 12, God is the one who will keep the message safe for Paul's successors, so that the gospel will outlast Paul's imprisonment.

views.label: Deliberately ambiguous
views.case: A few commentators suggest that Paul is happy to leave both senses open, since the life of the apostle and the message of the apostle were bound up together. The ambiguity does no harm because the same God guards both.

debates.bearing: The translation 'what I have entrusted' favours the first reading, but the repeated word in verse 14 favours the second. Either way, the guarding belongs to God first, which is why Timothy is told to guard only 'with the help of the Holy Spirit.'

study.originalLanguages:
Paul tells Timothy that 'God has not given us a spirit of fear.' The word for fear is deilia, and it names cowardice, the shrinking back of someone who lacks courage, more than mere nervousness. It is set against three gifts. 'Power' is dynamis, the strength of God at work; 'love' is agape, the self giving love that seeks another's good; and 'self-control' is a word of the sophron family, which describes a sound, steady mind and appears in Titus 2:2 and 2:5. The three together describe a mind that is steady under pressure.

'Testimony,' in verse 8, is martyrion, from which English takes 'martyr.' In Paul's day the word meant the witness a person bears, but its use in a letter written from a prison anticipates the later sense of one who bears witness at the cost of life. The 'holy calling' of verse 9 is a calling which comes from God's initiative, since 'called' (kaleo) in Paul's letters means a summons that actually brings its object into being, as in Romans 8:30.

The phrase 'before time began' renders a Greek phrase, pro chronon aionion, literally 'before ages of time.' Titus 1:2 uses the same expression, and the sense is that God's gift was planned before history began, not that grace existed in some mist before there were creatures. The 'appearing' of verse 10 is epiphaneia, a word Paul uses of Christ's first coming here and of His return in 2 Timothy 4:1 and 4:8 and Titus 2:13. In the first century it belonged to the language of a ruler's arrival and the manifestation of a god, so Paul takes a word of imperial pageant and gives it to Christ.

Verse 10 says Christ has 'abolished' death. The verb is katargeo, which means to render powerless or inoperative, not to cause to vanish. It matches the picture in 1 Corinthians 15:26, where death remains an enemy yet is sentenced to destruction, and in Hebrews 2:14, where the devil's hold is broken. The same verse says He 'illuminated' life and immortality, from photizo, to bring to light. Life was not created at the cross; it was made visible and available.

Finally, Paul writes 'I know whom I have believed,' using the perfect tense of oida for settled knowledge and the perfect of pisteuo for a trust that began at conversion and still stands. The 'treasure' or 'deposit' in verse 14 is paratheke, found in the New Testament only here, in verse 12 and in 1 Timothy 6:20, so it is a technical word for the apostolic message.

typology.type: A faith passed through three generations, Lois, Eunice and Timothy
typology.fulfillment: The household in verse 5 is a small picture of what God does with His covenant people from the start. Deuteronomy 6:6-7 tells parents to teach God's words to their children, and Psalm 78:5-7 shows the same pattern of one generation making known to the next. In Timothy that pattern is fulfilled in the New Covenant, where faith is no longer tied to being born into Israel, since Timothy's father was a Greek. The type is limited, because faith is never inherited by birth. It is 'sincere' only when it becomes the person's own, which is why Paul says 'is in you as well.'

typology.type: The deposit that must be guarded
typology.fulfillment: A deposit is the old picture of trust: something valuable left in another person's keeping. In Israel the law was kept in the ark, Deuteronomy 10:5, and later in the priests' and scribes' safekeeping. In Christ the pattern is brought to its fullest form, because the message entrusted to the apostles is about a Person and the keeping is done finally by Him. The apostle can trust his own life to One who 'is able to guard,' verse 12. The picture falls short where it might suggest that truth is kept by human vigilance alone. The Holy Spirit who dwells in the church is the guard, verse 14.

typology.type: Paul, the prisoner, as a living picture of the cross
typology.fulfillment: Paul calls himself 'His prisoner' and says he suffers for the gospel, verse 12. In Paul's chains the church sees a small, partial copy of Christ's shame and endurance, Hebrews 12:2. Philippians 3:10 speaks of sharing in His sufferings, and Colossians 1:24 of filling up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for His body. The comparison is not exact. Paul's sufferings do not atone, and Christ's alone were redemptive. But Paul shows what the cross looks like when it is carried instead of merely believed, which is exactly what he asks of Timothy.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ more directly than almost any part of the letter, because verses 9 and 10 are among the plainest statements in the Pastoral Letters of who He is and what He did. Paul writes of 'our Savior, Christ Jesus,' and the title 'Savior' is used in the same breath of God the Father in verse 9, 'He has saved us.' The Father saves and the Son is the Savior, and the letters never see these as rivals. Titus 2:13 and 3:4 to 6 make the same move of speaking of God our Savior and Jesus Christ our Savior within a few lines.

The chapter shows Christ first as the one in whom grace was given before time began. The grace of verse 9 was 'granted us in Christ Jesus' long before there were any people to receive it, so the plan of salvation does not wait on human performance and was never a rescue improvised after the fall. Ephesians 1:4 says we were chosen in Him before the foundation of the world. To say that grace was given 'in Christ' is to say that the Son was already the one in whom God meant to deal with sinners.

It then shows Christ as the one who came. 'Appearing' marks the incarnation as an arrival, the entrance of a king who has done what no earlier king could do. Death is not bypassed but 'abolished,' made powerless, in the same pattern as Hebrews 2:14, where the Son took on flesh and blood so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death. The resurrection is what makes the Savior's victory visible, and 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Him the firstfruits of those who sleep. To say He 'illuminated the way to life and immortality' is to say that the dark corridor of the grave now has a light at the end.

Christ is also the pattern of how the gospel is carried. Paul does not ask Timothy to do anything Christ did not do first. Christ endured the cross, scorning its shame, Hebrews 12:2, and so Timothy is not to be ashamed. Christ trusted His Father with His life, Luke 23:46, and so Paul can entrust his own. The words of Mark 8:38 hang behind the chapter: those who are ashamed of the Son of Man will find Him ashamed of them. The reverse is Paul's confidence in verse 12, that the One he has trusted will keep what has been put in His hand 'for that day,' the day of Christ's appearing.

A word of care is needed. The chapter does not say that a believer's suffering earns anything. The cross is complete, and Paul's chains are part of its proclamation, not an addition to its work. What the text offers instead is the link between the gospel and the life of its servants, so that the one who preaches the Savior who suffered should expect to share something of that road.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He acts before He is asked. 'He has saved us and called us,' Paul writes, and the reason is given negatively and positively: 'not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us.' God's purpose and grace are the whole explanation of salvation, and because they stand before time began they cannot be threatened by the failures of Timothy, Paul or the church in Asia. This is God's sovereignty put as pastoral comfort, since a plan that depends on God alone cannot be undone by fear.

He is a God of power and not only of tenderness. The spirit He gives is one of power, love and self-control, and Paul does not set power and love against one another. The power is 'the power of God' that carries Timothy through suffering, verse 8, and the love is what that power is for. This shapes how Christians understand strength: it is received, it is exercised for others, and it is steady under pressure.

God is faithful as a keeper. 'He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day,' verse 12. The Bible is full of the picture of God as one who keeps, from the blessing of Numbers 6:24 to Jude 24, and here Paul rests his hope on it. The phrase 'that day' reaches forward to judgment, and Paul is not afraid of it, because the Judge is the same Person he has trusted. The mention of 'that day' again in verse 18, when Paul prays that Onesiphorus will find mercy, shows that mercy is something one asks God for with confidence.

God is also the one who gives gifts and the one who reveals. He gave the gift in verse 6, the Spirit in verse 7 and the calling in verse 9, and He has now 'revealed' His grace. The Christian doctrine of revelation does not mean that God was hidden and needed finding; it means He chose to make visible what He had planned. The ordinary tone of the letter keeps this humble. God does not reveal Himself to impress but to rescue.

Verse 14 also gives a quiet glimpse of the Trinity at work: the Father who saves and calls, the Son who appears and abolishes death, and the Spirit who dwells in the believers and helps them guard what they were given. Nothing in the chapter is labelled as a doctrine of the Trinity, but all three Persons are named in a single movement of salvation and service.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to bring our fears to the God who has given something better in their place. We do not manufacture courage; we recall a God who planned our rescue before time, accomplished it by Christ's appearing, and keeps us until the day it is complete. The response is gratitude in the heart and steadiness in the hands.

crossReferences.note: Luke's account of Timothy's beginning. It names his Greek father and his believing Jewish mother, and says the brothers at Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him. It is the background for the Lois and Eunice of verse 5, and shows that Timothy's faith was recognised by the local church long before he served in Ephesus.

Describes the gift given to Timothy through prophecy and the laying on of the hands of the elders. Placed beside verse 6, it shows that Paul was not the only one who laid hands on Timothy, and that the gift is both a personal endowment and something the church had publicly recognised.

Paul's earlier public statement that he is not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation. The two ideas of shame and power sit together in 2 Timothy 1:7 and 1:8, so the older letter supplies the reason for the younger one's demand.

Jesus warns that anyone ashamed of Him and His words will find the Son of Man ashamed of him when He comes in glory. This is the weight behind Paul's command in verse 8, because the fear Paul names is not only a social one. It touches a person's standing on the last day.

Speaks of eternal life promised by God, who cannot lie, 'before time began.' The phrase matches verse 9 closely and helps explain it, since it ties the grace given before the ages to a promise that God made and can be counted on to keep.

Calls death 'the last enemy to be destroyed.' Together with verse 10, it shows what 'abolished' means. Death is already defeated in Christ's resurrection but still has to be removed finally, so the believer lives in the time between the sentence and its execution.

Explains how death is abolished: the Son shared flesh and blood so that through His own death He might break the devil's hold on death and free those held by fear of it. It is the other side of 2 Timothy 1:7, since the spirit of fear is answered by a Savior who has dealt with the thing feared.

Charges Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him and to avoid empty chatter. It uses the same word for deposit as 2 Timothy 1:14, and shows that guarding the gospel was a standing instruction in Paul's letters to Timothy, not a one off request from prison.

Tells those suffering according to God's will to entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and keep doing good. It is the best parallel for Paul's trust in verse 12, because it joins suffering, entrusting and the faithfulness of God in a single sentence.

Calls us to look to Jesus, who endured the cross 'scorning its shame.' Where Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed, Hebrews shows the One who treated shame as a small thing for the sake of the joy set before Him. It gives the fuller motive for the command.

Paul's own later account of being deserted at his first defense and yet stood by and strengthened by the Lord. It reads like a fulfilment of verse 12, where he said he knew whom he had trusted, and shows the guarding of God in practice.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a world that God made good and a people who lost it by distrust, and from then on its story is about what God does to bring them back. This chapter sits very late in that story, but it speaks to its earliest question: has God's plan been going on from the beginning, or was it an emergency measure? Paul answers that grace was given in Christ Jesus 'before time began,' verse 9, so that the rescue is older than the problem. The promise to the woman's seed in Genesis 3:15, the call of Abraham and the covenant with David were not improvisations but the unfolding of what was already purposed.

What the chapter answers from before is also the fear that death has the last word. Since Genesis 3 death has been the sentence on every life, and the Old Testament shows people longing for relief from it, in the psalms and in Job. Verse 10 says that death has now been made powerless and that life and immortality have been brought to light. The 'appearing' of Christ is the point where the long Old Testament hope turns into a fact.

It also sets up what follows. The gospel has been entrusted to a messenger, and the messenger to others, so the deposit passes from Paul to Timothy and from Timothy to faithful people who will teach others, 2 Timothy 2:2. The story of redemption now runs through ordinary people who guard and hand on. The household of Lois and Eunice and the single friend Onesiphorus are the way the story continues in the period between Christ's first and second appearing. Their faith will not be dramatic, but it is how the church arrives in every generation.

The chapter ends with a contrast that is also a part of the larger story: those who leave and those who stay. This repeats from Genesis to Revelation. In Eden two people hid from God. Israel at times turned away and at times came back. In the Gospels most of the disciples scattered when Jesus was arrested. Here the Asians scatter while Onesiphorus seeks Paul out. The Bible does not hide the cost of faithfulness, nor does it pretend the faithful are many.

It will end in new creation, which is why Paul looks forward to 'that day' twice in this chapter. On that day death is not only weakened but finally gone, Revelation 21:4, the guarded deposit is delivered and the mercy asked for Onesiphorus is found. Believers who have borne the shame of the gospel will see that it was the way to glory, and the One who was ashamed of no one who trusted Him will bring His people home.

sermon.title: The Good Deposit
sermon.why: Part of Begg's series A Study in 2 Timothy, this message expounds 2 Timothy 1:14-18, the charge to guard the good deposit by the Spirit's help, set against the deserters and the loyal Onesiphorus. A careful, orthodox treatment of the chapter's central theme of faithful stewardship of the gospel.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean when he tells Timothy to fan the gift into flame?

options.text: To actively stir up and use the grace God has given, not let it lie dormant.
options.note: The verb pictures rekindling living coals into full flame; grace must be exercised.

options.text: To wait passively until he feels more confident.
options.note: The image is active stirring, not passive waiting.

options.text: To seek a brand new gift he does not yet have.
options.note: The gift is already in him through the laying on of hands; it needs rekindling, not replacing.

options.text: To keep his gift hidden to avoid trouble.
options.note: The whole point is bold use, the opposite of hiding.

quiz.q: What kind of spirit has God given us, according to verse 7?

options.text: A spirit of timidity that keeps us safe and quiet.
options.note: Paul says God did not give a spirit of fear or cowardice.

options.text: A spirit of power, love, and self-control.
options.note: This is exactly the threefold gift Paul names against timidity.

options.text: A spirit of power only, so we can dominate others.
options.note: Power is named, but alongside love and self-control, not for domination.

options.text: A spirit of love and self-control, but not real power.
options.note: Love and self-control are named, but power is included too.

quiz.q: On what basis does God save and call us, according to verses 9 and 10?

options.text: By His own purpose and grace given in Christ before time began.
options.note: Verse 9 grounds salvation in God's eternal purpose and grace, not our works.

options.text: By our good works and sincere effort.
options.note: Paul explicitly says not because of our works.

options.text: By a mix of grace and our works together.
options.note: Paul rules out works as the basis; it is grace and God's purpose.

options.text: By His grace, revealed through the appearing of Christ our Savior.
options.note: True and central, though the fullest answer names God's eternal purpose behind that grace.

quiz.q: Why is Paul not ashamed even though he suffers in prison?

options.text: Because he knows whom he has believed and trusts Christ to guard the deposit.
options.note: Verse 12 grounds his confidence in the trustworthy Christ he knows.

options.text: Because his imprisonment is only a minor inconvenience.
options.note: Paul takes his suffering seriously; his confidence is in Christ, not in comfort.

options.text: Because he is sure Christ is able to keep what is entrusted for that day.
options.note: True, and part of the same verse, though the anchor is knowing Christ personally.

options.text: Because he expects to be released soon.
options.note: The letter shows Paul expecting death, not release; his hope is Christ.

quiz.q: How does the example of Onesiphorus function in the chapter?

options.text: He models the unashamed loyalty Paul calls for, refreshing Paul and seeking him out in Rome.
options.note: Onesiphorus embodies the courage set against the deserters of Asia.

options.text: He is a warning of how not to treat imprisoned believers.
options.note: He is a positive example, not a warning; the deserters are the warning.

options.text: He shows that some served Paul faithfully while others fell away.
options.note: True, and the contrast is real, though his main role is a model of courage.

options.text: He is praised mainly for his wealth and status.
options.note: He is praised for mercy and refreshing service, not status.

questions: Timothy's faith was nurtured by his grandmother and mother. Who has God used to hand faith down to you, and whom are you helping to pass it on to?
Paul says the gift of God can grow cold if it is not stirred up. Where in your walk with Christ do the coals need fanning back into flame right now?
God gives a Spirit of power, love, and self-control rather than fear. In which situation are you most tempted to shrink back in timidity, and how would those three gifts change your response?
Being ashamed of Christ often shows up in small silences. Where might you be quietly distancing yourself from Jesus or from other believers who are under pressure?
Paul entrusted both his future and the gospel to a God who keeps what is placed in His care. What are you finding hard to entrust to God today, and what would it mean to place it in His keeping?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes that the word rendered fear can also be translated timidity or cowardice; it names a shrinking fearfulness, the only occurrence of this Greek term in the New Testament.
The phrase what I have entrusted to Him can also be rendered what He has entrusted to me, as the BSB footnote observes; the two readings highlight God keeping us and us keeping the gospel.
The treasure entrusted translates the good deposit, the same Greek word used in verse 12, linking God's safekeeping of us with our safekeeping of the gospel.
The Province of Asia is literally Asia, a Roman province in what is now western Turkey, as the BSB footnote explains, not the modern continent.
